episode_title: Workplace Learning, Grounded in Science - AXIOM Insights Learning and Development Podcast episode 45

real_qa.q: What is the difference between learning in the flow of work versus learning through the flow of work according to cognitive science?
real_qa.r: Learning in the flow of work is often misinterpreted as ambient coaching or pop-ups that appear during task execution, but the foundational science from situated learning theory actually tells us that you learn through the process of working—the work itself, the actual execution and completion of tasks, is the learning activity. This occurs within a container involving a more experienced other like a manager or peer, and a community of practice at various stages of doing the work.
real_qa.requete: learning flow of work cognitive science difference

real_qa.q: How should L&D professionals respond when asked to teach a complex skill like innovation in a limited timeframe like four hours?
real_qa.r: Start by asking questions to understand what the organization actually hopes to achieve. If they want employees to show more innovative behaviors and mindsets, you can stress the importance and give people one or two applied things to practice. If they want substantial capability building toward behavior change, explain that this requires deliberate practice, time for cognitive and metacognitive reflection, and a paced strategy connected to real work moments with coaching and cultural reinforcement—and offer to design a different, more comprehensive innovation capability building strategy rather than attempting the impossible in four hours.
real_qa.requete: teach innovation four hours L&D strategy

real_qa.q: Why do L&D professionals continue to separate learning and performance despite decades of discussion about integrating them?
real_qa.r: The core issue is that learning is fundamentally a neurobiological process—the creation or strengthening of a pathway between two neurons, supported by specific neurochemicals and neurotransmitters—yet many L&D approaches neglect this neurobiology. When we artificially separate learning from doing, we accidentally box ourselves into content provision thinking rather than designing for how the brain actually learns, which requires understanding that neurobiological processes are influenced by environment and context. We keep replicating approaches that don't work because we lack this scientific grounding.
real_qa.requete: why L&D separates learning performance neurobiology

real_qa.q: What cognitive science principles does Axiom Insights' certificate in workplace learning teach L&D professionals?
real_qa.r: The certificate in workplace learning, created as part of the Next Level Lab at Harvard, is designed to help L&D professionals design learning that fits how and where people actually work, grounded in cognitive science, neuroscience, and learning design. The certificate focuses on evidence-based approaches to make workplace learning more continuous and embedded in how work actually happens, moving away from siloed content provision toward learning integrated into real performance contexts.
real_qa.requete: Axiom Insights certificate workplace learning Harvard

real_qa.q: How can L&D leaders shift their role from order-takers to strategic advisors in organizations?
real_qa.r: Grounding your approach in cognitive science and neurobiology gives you empirical data and evidence to support your recommendations when talking back to business leaders, rather than it sounding like opinion. Practice the mantra 'don't just take the order'—use a 'yes, and' approach where you fulfill immediate requests but frame something broader that will be successful over time. Work with VPs of Learning and Chief Learning Officer communities to collectively shift how the L&D function is perceived by understanding learning as a neurobiological process and designing accordingly.
real_qa.requete: L&D shift order-taker to strategic advisor

guest.titre: Cognitive Scientist, Leader of the Next Level Lab
guest.entreprise_secondaire: Harvard Innovation Lab (formerly Stanford University D School)
guest.bio_context: Dr. Forshaw is a cognitive scientist who leads the Next Level Lab at Harvard and was part of the team that created a new certificate in workplace learning focused on helping L&D professionals design learning grounded in cognitive science, neuroscience, and learning design. Before becoming an academic, she worked in a consulting firm for more than a decade doing learning and talent organization work, including capability building for ERP implementations and 21st century skills initiatives. She teaches innovation and creativity at the Harvard Innovation Lab and previously taught at Stanford University's D School.
